Everyone’s got a quick question.

And you shouldn’t have to answer them all.

Bill Guo, with Bryan

The problem

I became the team’s search engine

Every team has one person everyone reaches out to. They know where things live, why a decision went the way it did, and who to ask when you’re stuck. Our team has a few too many sports fans, so we call ours the GOAT.

I lead a remote design team of fifteen, and a lot of the team’s questions find their way to me. I went through two and a half years of requests — 2,413 of them — and sorted each by what it took to answer.

What was in my inbox

Did these all need me?

Just over half didn't need me at all. About a third needed only my sign-off once the groundwork was done. Roughly one in eight needed me from the start.

    The MVP for everyday questions

    Pilot test

    A tryout with the team

    I invited the whole team to ask le goat anything they used to bring to me, in Slack or in Figma. Within two weeks, they asked 228 questions, averaging 31 a day in week two. That’s more than three times my busiest week.

    They wanted it in the flow

    The funny thing about giving people an agent they can ask anything: they start wanting it everywhere.

    le goat in Figma comments

    Ask in the thread. It answers there.

    Reflection

    Setting the GOAT free

    Every team needs someone who knows where things live, why decisions were made, and who owns what. But their days shouldn’t go to answering the same questions.

    le goat takes care of the everyday asks, freeing those people for the work that needs them: hard design calls, riffing on ideas, pushing boundaries, and raising the ceiling.

    There’s a bigger benefit, too. As agents become part of everyday work, a reliable knowledge base matters even more. Fewer discrepancies mean fewer made-up answers and better information for people and agents alike.

    Let le goat handle the busywork, so the real GOATs have time for the hard work.
